items.title: 4.2 Solution of First-Order and First-Degree Differential Equations

source_refs.note: Book p. 129 (PDF 131): 4.2 general form dy/dx = f(x,y), differential form M dx + N dy = 0, Examples (i)-(ii), solution, initial value condition, IVP; text before 4.2.1

blocks.text: General form of the first order and first degree differential equations.

blocks.text_alt: d y by d x equals f of x and y

blocks.text: where \(f\) is a function of two variables \(x\) and \(y\), defined on some region of the \(xy\)-plane. It is always possible to write the above equation in differential form as follows:

blocks.text_alt: M of x and y times d x plus N of x and y times d y equals zero

blocks.text: where \(M(x, y)\) and \(N(x, y)\) are the functions of \(x\) and \(y\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Recall from 4.1: "first order" means the highest derivative in the equation is \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) (no \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) or higher). "First degree" means \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) appears only to the power 1 (no \(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\)). So every equation in this section can be solved for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and written as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\).
Why two forms? The form \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\) shows the rate of change clearly; the differential form \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\) is handy when we want to separate or integrate. They carry the same information:
\[M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{M}{N}, \quad N \ne 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the book changes (i) into differential form (the step it leaves out): cross-multiply, then bring every term to one side.
\[(y - x)\,dy = (x + y)\,dx\]
\[(x + y)\,dx - (y - x)\,dy = 0\]
\[(x + y)\,dx + (x - y)\,dy = 0\]
The last line uses \(-(y - x) = x - y\). For (ii): \(y\,dy = -x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx + y\,dy = 0\). Here \(M = x\) and \(N = y\).
A solution of a differential equation is a function defined on some interval \(I\) that reduces the equation to an identity. A condition of the form

\[y = y_0 \ \text{at} \ x = x_0\]
written as
\[y(x_0) = y_0\]
is called an initial value condition or one point boundary condition. A differential equation together with an initial value condition is called an Initial Value Problem (IVP).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What "reduces the equation to an identity" means: put the function and its derivative into the equation; both sides become exactly the same expression for every \(x\) in \(I\).
Our own illustration: for \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x\), the function \(y = x^2 + c\) is a solution for every constant \(c\), because \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^2 + c) = 2x\). This whole family (one curve for each \(c\)) is the general solution.
If we also demand \(y(0) = 3\) (an IVP), then \(3 = 0 + c\), so \(c = 3\) and the one curve we want is \(y = x^2 + 3\): the particular solution. The initial condition picks one curve, the one passing through the point \((x_0, y_0)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What comes next: this section solves two kinds of first-order, first-degree equations.
4.2.1 Separable: the right side splits as (function of \(x\)) \(\times\) (function of \(y\)).
4.2.2 Homogeneous: the right side depends only on the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\); the substitution \(y = vx\) turns it into a separable equation.
So the first job in every question is the same: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\) and look carefully at \(f\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A first-order, first-degree equation can always be written as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\) or as \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\).
2. A solution is a function that makes the equation an identity on an interval \(I\).
3. The general solution contains one arbitrary constant; it is a family of curves.
4. An initial value condition \(y(x_0) = y_0\) fixes that constant. Equation + initial condition = Initial Value Problem (IVP).
5. In an IVP, first find the general solution, then substitute \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) to find the constant.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Losing a sign when changing to differential form: from \((y - x)\,dy = (x + y)\,dx\) the term moved across changes sign.
2. Reading \(y(x_0) = y_0\) as "y times \(x_0\)". It means: the value of \(y\) when \(x = x_0\).
3. Forgetting the arbitrary constant: without it you have only one solution, not the general solution, and an IVP cannot be solved.
